title: In the beginning (Genesis 1:1–5)
hook: darkness on the deep, the Spirit over the waters, and let there be light

segments.voice: Yesterday, the canon: a library of seventy-three. Which unfamiliar book did you find on the shelf? Today we take down the first one and open it to the first line. Day three hundred thirty-three.

It's the night before Easter. The church is completely dark. People stand in the doorway holding unlit candles. Outside, a fire is struck, a single tall candle is lit from it, and a deacon carries it slowly up the aisle, singing. The flame passes from wick to wick until the whole room glows. Then everyone sits down, and the first reading of that long night begins. Of all the pages in the library, the Church chooses this one to read first in the dark: the opening of Genesis. In the beginning.
screen: `THE EASTER VIGIL, IN THE DARK.` → `ONE CANDLE, THEN A ROOM OF THEM.` → `THE FIRST READING: GENESIS.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims Bible, the old Catholic English translation, opens like this: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." In Hebrew, in the beginning is a single word, bereshit, and it gives the whole book its Hebrew name. Then the scene, and it's not tidy at all. The earth is void and empty, darkness is on the face of the deep, and the spirit of God moves over the waters. The Hebrew word for spirit, ruach, also means wind and breath. So before anything has a shape, something is already moving over the dark water. Next, God speaks. In the Douay-Rheims, the line is famous for how short it is: "Be light made. And light was made." A three-word command, and the result in four. No battle, no raw material wrestled into shape. A word, and then light. God sees that the light is good, separates it from the darkness, and calls one day and the other night. Then a detail that's easy to miss: the sun and moon don't appear until the fourth day. Light comes before anything that shines. The Catechism teaches that the world begins in God's wisdom and love, not in accident or struggle. And Catholics hear the same opening again at Christmas, in the Gospel of John: in the beginning was the Word. At the Vigil, on the night the Church celebrates the resurrection, the readings go back to the first light.
screen: `BERESHIT: IN THE BEGINNING.` · `SPIRIT, WIND, BREATH OVER THE DEEP.` · `BE LIGHT MADE. AND LIGHT WAS MADE.` · `LIGHT BEFORE THE SUN.` · then, large: `LET THERE BE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: switch on a light slowly, on purpose. If you can, find a lamp or a switch near you, and sit in whatever dimness the room gives you. Settle, and breathe. Notice what the dark does: the edges go soft, the room gets quieter. Then reach for the switch, slowly, and turn it on. Watch what appears: colors, faces in photos, the mess on the table, all of it there the whole time. If you pray, you can say the old line silently: be light made. If not, just notice the difference light makes. The bell holds the time.
In the beginning. Bereshit in Hebrew: the Bible's first word, and the Hebrew name of Genesis. Before anything, God speaking light into the dark.
Your line: let there be light. Today, each time you flip a switch, let it remind you of the first thing God says in Genesis: be light made. Day three hundred thirty-three.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 1:1 and 1:3 quoted from memory of the Challoner text; confirm punctuation exactly.

'The Catechism calls the light God's first creation': CCC 298 speaks of God creating light (with reference to 2 Corinthians 4:6); CCC 295 on creation from God's wisdom and love. Confirm the paraphrase is fair or soften.
Easter Vigil: Genesis 1:1–2:2 is the first of up to seven Old Testament readings; confirm. The Gospel of John 1:1–18 is the Gospel of Christmas Day Mass.

Editor review (days 333-350): fixed the word count of the Douay-Rheims line ('Be light made' is three words, not four); cut the unsupported 'the Church has always read' and the claim that the Catechism calls light God's first creation; dropped the causal 'that's why the Vigil starts here'; the carry no longer says light was the first thing God made (heaven and earth come in 1:1).
